title: UX Designer Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)
meta_description: A complete UX designer resume example: portfolio case studies, user research, wireframes, design systems, and the exact bullet formula that turns design work into proof hiring managers and applicant tracking systems both reward.
content_html:
UX Designer Resume Example & Writing Guide (2026)

A UX designer resume has one job: prove you can make products easier to use, not just prettier to look at. Hiring managers do not hire for tool lists, Dribbble shots, or pleasant adjectives alone. They hire for problems found, flows fixed, tests run, and outcomes measured: the friction you spotted, the change you made, and the result that followed.

Quick answer: A UX designer resume should include a portfolio link with 3 to 4 case studies, a summary naming the products you designed for and your strongest outcome, a skills section with user research, wireframing, prototyping, and usability testing, experience bullets pairing each design task with the outcome it produced, and the tools you genuinely use.

Key Takeaways

  • Every experience bullet follows the same formula: problem + action + outcome — the friction you found, the flow you fixed, the drop-off you cut.
  • Lead with your portfolio and your outcome: onboarding rebuilt, checkout drop-off cut by a third, task success lifted from 6 in 10 to 9 in 10.
  • Spell tools exactly as postings do — Figma, Maze, Miro, Adobe XD — they are literal ATS keyword filters.
  • Show impact through counts, percentages, and ranges, never through confidential details: name the result, withhold the private detail.
  • Keep the file itself single-column with standard headings and real text, so applicant tracking systems parse it cleanly.

What Hiring Managers Actually Look For

Ask a hiring manager what separates a keep-forever UX designer from a risky one and it won’t be “great eye for design.” It’ll be:

  • Problems that actually get solved. Flows that got shorter, tasks that got easier, drop-offs that shrank — not screens that look busy and change nothing.
  • Research that finds real friction. Users watched and listened to, not assumptions dressed as insight, and findings that changed the design.
  • Prototypes that get tested. Ideas put in front of users early, tested honestly, and iterated on instead of defended.
  • Systems thinking. Components reused, patterns documented, and designs that scale instead of one-off screens.
  • Stakeholders who stay aligned. Product managers briefed properly, engineers consulted early, and trade-offs explained honestly.

UX Designer Resume Example (Annotated)

Below is an example for a UX designer working on consumer apps. It’s fictional — names and companies are illustrative — but every bullet follows the pattern hiring managers respond to: problem, action, outcome.

AMARA OKONKWO
Lagos · (234) 555-0119 · amara.okonkwo@email.com · amaraokonwodesign.com · linkedin.com/in/amaraokonkwo

SUMMARY
UX designer with 5 years designing fintech and retail apps, currently owning end-to-end UX for a payments app used by 40,000 people a month. Cut onboarding drop-off from 4 in 10 to 1 in 10 and built the team’s first design system in Figma. Known for flows that get shorter and screens that survive real users.

SKILLS
User research · Wireframing · Prototyping · Usability testing · Information architecture · Interaction design · Design systems · Accessibility (WCAG) · Figma · Sketch · Adobe XD · Miro · Maze · Notion

PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE

Senior UX Designer — PayNest, Lagos | 2022–Present

  • Own end-to-end UX for a payments app used by 40,000 people a month: research, flows, prototypes, and usability testing, with onboarding drop-off cut from 4 in 10 to 1 in 10.
  • Redesigned the checkout flow after watching 30 users struggle with it, cutting the steps from 7 to 4 and lifting completed payments by a third.
  • Run usability tests every sprint with 8 to 12 participants, turning the top findings into fixes within the same sprint instead of a backlog that never clears.
  • Built the team’s first design system in Figma — 60 components, documented patterns — so new screens ship in half the time and look like one product.
  • Led the onboarding redesign that cut support tickets about setup by half, after interviews showed new users could not find the first step.

UX Designer — Brightline Studio, Lagos | 2020–2022

  • Designed flows and prototypes for 6 client apps — onboarding, booking, and checkout — testing each with 5 to 8 users before handover.
  • Mapped user journeys for a food-delivery app, finding 3 drop-off points the client had missed and redesigning the worst one first.
  • Ran card sorts and tree tests that cut a retail app’s navigation from 12 top-level items to 5, with task success up from 6 in 10 to 9 in 10.

EDUCATION
BA, Visual Communication — 2020

Section-by-Section Breakdown

Summary: products designed, tenure, and headline proof in three lines

The example opens with the products designed and tenure, then the proof: drop-off cut, design system built, tests run every sprint. Without UX experience yet, lead with equivalent scope: “mapped the sign-up flow for a student project, tested it with 12 users, and cut the steps from 9 to 5.”

Skills: tools and duties exactly as postings spell them

Design postings are keyword-dense, and applicant tracking systems screen for exact terms. Name your tools (Figma, Maze, Miro) and your duties (user research, wireframing, usability testing). “Creative thinker” is not a keyword; “usability testing” is.

Experience: every bullet pairs a design task with the outcome gained

The pattern is problem + action + outcome: “cut checkout from 7 steps to 4 by watching 30 users struggle with it”; “lifted completed payments by a third by rebuilding the flow around what the tests showed.” Scope matters too — users reached, tests run, screens shipped, systems built.

Impact: show it through counts and percentages, never through secrets

Every designer claims impact; the strong ones prove it by naming the result and withholding the confidential detail: drop-off cut, task success lifted, tickets reduced. One bullet about a flow rebuilt proves the judgment hiring managers pay for, and separates a UX designer resume from a portfolio link with no story.

UX Designer Skills & ATS Keywords

Mirror the posting’s exact language and keep these groups on your resume:

  • Research & discovery: user research, interviews, surveys, usability testing, journey mapping, personas, Maze, Miro (only the depth you genuinely have).
  • Design & prototyping: wireframing, prototyping, interaction design, information architecture, Figma, Sketch, Adobe XD.
  • Systems & craft: design systems, accessibility (WCAG), typography, responsive design, handoff, Figma variables.
  • Tools: Figma, Sketch, Adobe XD, Miro, Maze, Notion, Slack, Zoom.

Check your resume against a free ATS scan — for example, Cvyon's ATS grader — before you apply. UX designer resumes fail most often on vague bullets and missing keywords, not on formatting. Start from a clean template gallery or resume builder option, then verify with the free ATS grader.

5 Mistakes That Cost UX Designer Interviews

  1. Portfolio link missing or broken. A UX resume without a working portfolio link is a claim with no evidence. Put the link at the top, test it, and make sure the case studies open without a password wall.
  2. Process without outcomes. “Ran workshops and made wireframes” says nothing about what changed. Every bullet needs a problem, an action, and a result.
  3. Jargon without results. “Leveraged design thinking to drive synergy” means nothing to a hiring manager. Name the friction, the fix, and the result: drop-off cut, task success lifted, tickets reduced.
  4. Tools without matching bullets. A software list proves nothing on its own. Pair each tool with work that used it: the prototype built, the test run, the system maintained.
  5. Unreadable formatting. Multi-column layouts, text boxes, and image-based PDFs scramble parsing, so your research section arrives as word soup. One column, standard headings, real text.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should be included in a UX designer resume?

A link to your portfolio with 3 to 4 case studies; a summary naming the products you designed for and your strongest outcome; a skills section with user research, wireframing, prototyping, usability testing, and design systems; experience bullets pairing each design task with the outcome it produced; and the tools you genuinely use, spelled exactly as postings spell them. A portfolio proves the craft; the resume proves the judgment behind it.

Do I need a degree to become a UX designer?

Not always — UX designers come from graphic design, psychology, research, front-end development, customer support, and bootcamp programs, and many enter through a junior or internship role plus a portfolio of real case studies. Hiring managers weigh the portfolio and the outcomes in it far more than a specific degree. A design or psychology degree helps for some employers, but a flow redesigned, a test run, and a drop-off cut prove more.

How do I show UX impact without revealing client work?

Use counts, percentages, and ranges instead of names: “redesigned the checkout flow and cut drop-off by a third” or “ran usability tests with 40 participants and fixed the top 5 issues” proves impact without naming a single client, product, or figure that was not public. Never share screenshots, data, or figures from work under NDA. Hiring managers read impact as judgment: the result stated plainly, the confidential detail withheld, and the scale implied by the work itself.

What is the difference between a UX designer and a UI designer resume?

A UX designer resume proves ownership of the experience: research, flows, prototypes, testing, and the outcomes that followed. A UI designer resume proves ownership of the interface: visual craft, design systems, typography, and polish. The UX resume names the problem found and the behaviour changed; the UI resume names the screens built and the system maintained. Many roles blend both, so lead with the side the posting asks for.

How do I write a UX designer resume with no UX title yet?

Lead with the closest equivalent work: the flows you mapped, the tests you ran, the prototypes you built, or the users you interviewed — then frame each as UX in miniature. “Mapped the sign-up flow for a student project, tested it with 12 users, and cut the steps from 9 to 5” proves the same skills at smaller scale. Add a portfolio with 3 case studies, run your resume through a free ATS grader first, and target junior UX or product design roles as stepping stones.

Should a UX designer resume list design tools?

Yes — tool keywords are literal ATS filters in design roles. List design and research tools (Figma, Sketch, Adobe XD, Miro, Maze) exactly as postings spell them, and only tools you genuinely use. A tool without a matching bullet reads thin, so pair each one with work that used it: the prototype built, the test run, the system maintained.
